overview: The Vandals established a kingdom centred on Carthage after its capture in 439. They ruled a population with older African and Roman institutions, languages and livelihoods. The imported map shows 500 to 600, but the kingdom was conquered in 533 and 534; the later part of that interval belongs to a different political order.

periods.title: A kingdom based at Carthage
periods.summary: The conquest brought a new dynasty into a region with cities, estates and Mediterranean connections.

periods.title: Court, commerce and religious competition
periods.summary: Latin public life and regional production continued under Vandal kings.

periods.title: Byzantine conquest and its aftermath
periods.summary: Belisarius defeated the kingdom; Eastern Roman rule replaced it in 534.

items.text: Capturing Carthage gave Vandal rulers access to an established maritime world. Historian Philip de Souza argues that crews already combined trading, ferrying, fishing and raiding, and continued these activities under new masters. Naval power depended on people with practical sea skills.

Vandal civil administration drew on Roman models and employed Romano-Africans. Surviving royal laws were written in Latin. Political conquest did not require replacing every clerk, legal formula or office with something newly invented.

North Africa remained multilingual. Latin, Punic and Amazigh languages had different geographical and social roles. A Latin royal inscription therefore cannot tell us what every farmer, sailor or family spoke at home.

The Albertini wooden tablets preserve land transactions from the 490s. They record local legal business and cultivated property under Vandal rule, providing a view of rural life that differs from chronicles focused on armies and kings.

Some of those documents identify widows as heads of households, while wives appear alongside husbands in transactions. These specific records show women participating in property arrangements; they do not establish that all women enjoyed equal wealth or authority.

African tableware continued crossing the Mediterranean. Late fifth- and early sixth-century deposits at Tarragona and Can Modolell contain recognizable African red-slip pottery forms, evidence that production and commercial connections survived the change of regime.

The pottery study finds continuity and expansion in these western Mediterranean imports after the Vandal kingdom consolidated. That conclusion concerns particular ceramic markets; it does not prove that every household prospered or every trade route behaved alike.

sections.title: Religion, leisure and small written messages

items.text: The ruling dynasty supported Homoian Christianity, while many churchmen defended the Nicene creed. Their dispute concerned how Christ related to God the Father. Both sides were Christian, and competition involved arguments about doctrine as well as political power.

The poet Luxorius celebrated gardens, baths and weddings associated with Vandal elites and also wrote pointed satirical verses. His poetry reveals social pleasures and rivalries in sixth-century Carthage, though elite entertainment is not a complete picture of ordinary life.

A small Latin sample on Hilderic’s silver coin is “FELIX KARTG”, meaning “fortunate Carthage”. The coin was struck at Carthage between 523 and 530 and shows the city personified. A place could appear on money as a human figure.

The same coin calls its king “D N HILDI-RIX REX”, expanded as Dominus Noster Hildirix Rex: “Our lord King Hilderic”. Royal money joined an individual ruler’s name with Roman-style titles and a familiar city image.

Researchers compare coin dies and buried coin groups to work out the order and dates of Vandal issues. Coins are useful evidence for government and exchange, but disputed sequences remind us that a small object does not arrive with its own complete history.

ending.text: Belisarius’s army conquered the Vandal kingdom in 533 and 534 and established Eastern Roman rule. The dynasty lost power, but African communities, Latin writing, farming and urban life continued through further changes. The map’s 600 endpoint is not a later Vandal survival date.
